title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An attorney submitted fake legal case citations to a court, generated by an artificial intelligence system, in a memorandum supporting his client's position in a civil dispute. The citations referenced two nonexistent cases. The failure was a deployment without human verification at the point of use, where a lawyer submitted AI-generated material to a court without checking whether the cases cited actually existed.

What caught this was opposing counsel and the judge identifying the citations as false during the case. The system that generated the citations asserted nonexistent cases as fact. This could have been prevented by a basic check against legal databases before filing, a standard part of legal practice that the AI system does not replace.

It is not established whether the AI system was designed to generate plausible-sounding but false citations, or whether it failed in a task it was intended to perform correctly.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for 30 days after submitting fake legal case citations generated by artificial intelligence in court filings. Ahmed cited two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in a 2025 memorandum filed in Hennepin County Court to support his client's position in a civil dispute. The lawyer also included a false quotation from a real case and made citation errors. Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client, ordering defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent, and fined Ahmed $5,000 before referring him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board.

The Minnesota Supreme Court's disciplinary office pursued action against Ahmed, noting his conduct caused unnecessary delay and required opposing counsel and the court to expend extra effort identifying nonexistent cases. Ahmed agreed to the 30-day suspension and must pay an additional $900 in costs. This case reflects a growing problem with AI-generated fake legal citations, with over 800 documented instances catalogued on a dedicated website. State officials emphasized that attorneys' ethical obligations regarding competent representation and truthfulness apply regardless of whether they use artificial intelligence tools.
